title: Twelve steps
hookLine: Alcoholics Anonymous blends honesty, surrender and service, with a "higher power" each person defines

lines: A FIRST NAME, A HARD SENTENCE.
A NUMBERED LIST ON THE WALL.
cards: A church basement on a weeknight. Folding chairs in a circle, a coffee urn hissing in the corner, a plate of cookies nobody has touched yet.
Someone stands, says their first name, and then a sentence that may have taken years to say out loud. The room answers with their name, warmly.
Nobody asks what they do for a living, or which church, if any, they belong to. The church only lends the room.
On the wall there may be a poster with a numbered list: a spiritual path that grew up outside any one religion, in rooms like this one.

teach.h: STEP ONE: AN ADMISSION, NOT STRENGTH.
teach.b: The twelve steps come from Alcoholics Anonymous, whose founders are known as Bill W. and Dr. Bob.

In plain paraphrase: It begins not with strength but with an admission: I'm powerless over alcohol, and my life has become unmanageable. Then: I've come to believe a power greater than myself could restore me to sanity.

teach.h: GOD, AS EACH PERSON UNDERSTANDS GOD.
teach.b: Then a decision to turn my will and my life over to the care of God, as each person understands God. The steps don't say which God. Some members mean the God of their childhood faith.
Some mean nature, or love. Some, by their own account, mean the group itself.
The middle steps make honesty concrete: a searching moral inventory, written down, then admitted to God, to yourself and to one other human being.
Then a list of everyone you've harmed, and amends wherever they won't cause more harm. The last step is service: carrying the message to someone still struggling. Surrender, honesty, repair, service.
Holding it all up is a saying you'll hear in those rooms: one day at a time. Not forever. Just today.

teach.h: TAKE THEREFORE NO THOUGHT FOR THE MORROW.
teach.b: The saying has an older cousin in the Gospels: "Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself." Neither line says tomorrow doesn't matter.
Both say it can't be carried today. AA's own tradition says the only requirement for joining is a desire to stop drinking.
If drinking or drugs are a struggle for you, that door is open, and other fellowships adapt the same steps.

how: People in Alcoholics Anonymous and other twelve-step fellowships attend meetings, work through the steps with a sponsor who has walked them before, and practice service by helping newcomers, taking recovery one day at a time.

s: AA requires members to believe in one particular God
it speaks of God as each person understands God. some members mean the group itself.
the steps begin with an admission of powerlessness
not with strength: I'm powerless, and my life has become unmanageable.
the last step is about keeping your recovery private

games.q: you've tried for years to stop drinking by willpower alone, and it keeps failing. what does step one ask?
o: admit you're powerless over it and your life has become unmanageable.
wait until you feel strong enough.
games.why: the twelve steps start with defeat, honestly admitted. in AA's telling, that admission is where change begins.

practice: Ask quietly what you're trying to control on your own that isn't working, a habit, a worry, a person, and let one thing come forward.
Picture holding it in your hands, then setting it down before whatever you trust: God, if you pray; the people who love you; life itself. You're not giving up on it, only giving up carrying it alone.

wordCard.voice: Twelve steps. The path of Alcoholics Anonymous: admit powerlessness, turn to a greater power, take an honest inventory, make amends, carry the message on. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: one day at a time. Not forever, just the day in front of you. See you tomorrow.
